_comment: Guided tour: a real cryo-EM map from EMDB and the atomic model deposited with it. EMD-3061 and PDB 5A63 are the same experiment -- human gamma-secretase at 3.4 A -- so the model belongs in the map and every number has a right answer to check against. Steps point at real controls and wait for the user to run the command; nothing is pressed on their behalf. Read by chimol.tour.
title: Fit a model into a cryo-EM map

steps.title: A map and the model that belongs in it
steps.text:
EMD-3061 is human gamma-secretase at 3.4 angstrom. PDB 5A63 is the model built into that very map, so this tour has a right answer to check against -- which is the only way to learn what a good fit looks like.

Ten steps. You run the commands; the tour points at where they go.

steps.title: Fetch the map
steps.text:
EMDB entries are fetched by accession, exactly like a PDB entry. The map arrives with its own voxel size and origin and lands where the file says it does -- not at the scene origin, which is the difference between a density around a model and one beside it.

About 20 MB the first time; it is cached afterwards.
steps.hint: Type fetch EMD-3061 at the prompt, or use File to open a local .map file.

steps.title: Look at what arrived
steps.text: Before contouring anything, read the map: its size in voxels, its step, its origin, and the range of its values. The contour level you are about to choose is a number in that range, and a level outside it is the usual reason a contour comes out empty.

steps.title: Contour it
steps.text:
A map is drawn by choosing one value and showing the surface where the density crosses it. The default is the level EMDB's depositors recommended for this entry when there is one -- they chose it for this map, which beats any rule of thumb.

The Map panel plots the value distribution with each contour marked on it, so the level can be chosen by looking rather than by guessing and re-rendering.

steps.title: The panel that chooses the level for you
steps.text: Contouring by typing a number means guessing, rendering, and guessing again. The Density panel plots the map's value distribution with each contour marked on it, so a level is chosen by looking.\n\nThe histogram is where the map's noise ends and its density begins; drag a marker and the contour follows.
steps.hint: Drag a marker on the histogram, or type volume_level EMD-3061, 0.06.

steps.title: Remove the dust
steps.text: Every real map has specks: isolated blobs of noise that clear the contour level and clutter the picture. hide_dust drops the connected pieces smaller than a size you give, keeping the ones that are actually the molecule. It takes the map, not the contour object you just named: the dust is a property of the density. Start around 30 angstrom and raise it until only the structure is left. This changes the picture, not the data.
steps.hint: Type hide_dust EMD-3061, 30 -- the map, not the contour object. Raise the number if specks remain.

steps.title: Now the model
steps.text: 5A63 is the model deposited with this map. It arrives in the map's own coordinate frame, so it is already sitting inside the density -- which is what a correct fit looks like. Worth doing now: run the fit before moving anything. It moves the model 0.03 angstrom and 0.1 degree, i.e. it agrees that the deposited position is the answer. A fit that cannot leave a correct model alone is no use for finding an incorrect one.

steps.title: Move it, so there is something to fit
steps.text:
A fit is only convincing if you have seen it recover from a known error. Push the model out of the density by a few angstrom and a few degrees -- both, since a rigid-body fit has to solve for both.

Watch the model leave the map.
steps.hint: Type translate [6, -4, 3], 5a63, then rotate x, 8, 5a63 if you want a rotation too.

steps.title: Fit it back
steps.text: fitmap follows the density's gradient at the atoms and the torque it exerts about the model's own centre, moving the model rigidly. Given a resolution it also reports a map-to-map correlation: the model's own simulated density against this map, voxel by voxel. That is the number to quote. Do not expect 1.0 on a real map. Against a simulated one a perfect fit scores 1.000, but an experimental map carries solvent, noise and density the model does not account for -- this pair scores about 0.49 at its best. What matters is that the number is at its maximum, which is why you compare it before and after. It finds the nearest maximum, not the best one. A 45 degree error comes back; 90 degrees does not, and still reports an ordinary-looking score.
steps.hint: Type fitmap 5a63, EMD-3061, 3.4 and watch it return to the density.

steps.title: What the model would look like as a map
steps.text: The other direction, and the check worth knowing: molmap simulates the density this model would give at a stated resolution. Contour it beside the real one and the two should agree. That is also what the correlation you just read is computed from, so this is the picture behind the number.
steps.hint: Type molmap 5a63, 3.4, sim, then isomesh msh, sim to see it.
